decks.title: Political Theory: An Introduction, Part 1: What Is Politics?
goals: Describe the popular view of politics and the wider view
Explain the idea of Aristotle that humans are political by nature
Give the standard definition of politics and its parts
Show with examples that politics appears in the family, the school, the market and the government
Explain why politics touches the life of every person

slides.heading: What Is Politics?
slides.body_md: Part 1: how people **see** politics, how thinkers **widen** that view, and a **standard definition**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: popular views, wider views, the definition, and politics everywhere
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: What is politics? Many people think of scheming and quarrels. In this part we compare that popular view with a wider view, learn the standard definition of politics, and see how politics appears in the family, the school, the market and the government.

slides.heading: Two views of politics

headers: What politics is taken to be
rows: Manipulation, scheming or the pursuit of self-interest by politicians
It leaves out the many useful decisions that groups take together
The activity through which a society makes collective decisions, settles differences and pursues common goals
Nothing essential: it covers families, schools, markets and governments

visual.alt: Table comparing two views of politics. The popular view takes politics to be manipulation, scheming or the pursuit of self-interest by politicians, and leaves out the many useful decisions groups take together. The wider view takes politics to be the activity through which a society makes collective decisions, settles differences and pursues common goals, covering families, schools, markets and governments

slides.narration: Many people think politics means manipulation, scheming and the pursuit of self interest by politicians. That is the popular view. The wider view says that politics is the activity through which a society makes collective decisions, settles differences and pursues common goals. The wider view covers families, schools, markets and governments.

slides.heading: Answering the popular view

rows: Politics is only about parties and elections
Any group that decides together engages in politics
Misuse of power by some is a fault of conduct; the need for shared decisions remains
Every person lives under shared decisions, so politics touches everyone

visual.alt: Table of three common claims about politics and the reply from the wider view: politics is only about parties and elections, but any group that decides together engages in politics; politics is always dirty, but misuse of power by some is a fault of conduct while the need for shared decisions remains; politics is not my concern, but every person lives under shared decisions

slides.narration: Three claims are often heard. First, that politics is only about parties and elections. Second, that it is always dirty. Third, that it is not our concern. The wider view replies that any group which decides together engages in politics, that misuse of power is a fault of conduct, and that shared decisions touch every person.

slides.heading: Aristotle: humans are political beings

rows: Aristotle, a thinker of ancient Greece
Human beings are by nature political: they live in communities and share in decisions about common life
Community life and public decisions are part of being human, not an accident

visual.alt: Table on Aristotle: a thinker of ancient Greece; his idea is that human beings are political by nature, living in communities and sharing in decisions about common life; the implication is that community life and public decisions are part of being human

slides.narration: Aristotle was a thinker of ancient Greece. He held that human beings are political by nature. We live together in communities and share in decisions about our common life. So community life and public decisions are part of being human, and not an accident.

In a market, traders settle who gets which stall. In government, laws and budgets are decided. Each is a group making collective decisions.

slides.heading: The standard definition of politics

rows: A group decides for all its members
A school council votes on a canteen rule
Members hold different views and settle them
Some want snacks kept, others removed
Shares of benefits, duties and places are fixed
Stalls in a market lane are allotted
Someone or some body has the ability to decide
A club president alone decides who speaks

visual.alt: Table of the parts of the definition of politics: collective decision, as when a school council votes on a canteen rule; differences resolved, as when some want snacks kept and others removed; who gets what, as when stalls in a market lane are allotted; and the use of power, as when a club president alone decides who speaks
visual.caption: Politics is the process by which groups make collective decisions about how to live together, who gets what, and how power is used.

slides.narration: Politics is the process by which groups make collective decisions about how to live together, who gets what, and how power is used. It has four parts: a collective decision, differences that are resolved, a share of benefits and duties, and the use of power.

slides.heading: Quick check: where is politics found?
slides.body_md: Decide whether the statement is true or false.
slides.narration: Think about where politics can be found. Is it only in government offices?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a school council decides
slides.body_md: Show the features of politics in an imagined school council.

headers: Step in the imagined Pinecrest School council
rows: Members disagree about fried snacks in the canteen
They discuss and give reasons for each side
They vote and the rule applies to every student
A collective decision binding the group
The rule decides what every student may buy

visual.alt: Worked example table for the imagined Pinecrest School council: members disagree about fried snacks, showing differences of view; they discuss and give reasons, showing the settling of differences by argument; they vote and the rule applies to every student, showing a collective decision; and the rule decides what every student may buy, showing who gets what
visual.caption: Pinecrest School and its council are imagined.

slides.narration: In the imagined Pinecrest School, council members disagree about fried snacks in the canteen. They discuss, give reasons and vote. The rule then applies to every student. We can see differences of view, settling by argument, a collective decision, and a decision about who gets what.

slides.heading: Politics in the family

rows: A weekly talk and a rota
Yes: shares of duties are fixed together
Yes: a collective decision on resources
No: not a decision of the group

visual.alt: Table of family matters: sharing chores by a weekly talk and rota is politics in the wider sense; using the monthly savings by discussion and a vote is politics in the wider sense; choosing what one person wears, decided by the person alone, is not a decision of the group and so not politics in this sense

slides.narration: A family can practise politics in the wider sense. Sharing chores by a weekly talk and a rota is a collective decision. Using monthly savings after discussion and a vote is a decision on resources. But one person choosing what to wear alone is not a decision of the group, so it is not politics in this sense.

slides.heading: Politics in school, market and government

headers: Who gets what or who decides
rows: Which students may use the library and when
Who gets the best places in the lane
How public money is shared among services

visual.alt: Table of three settings: in a school, a council fixes library hours and so decides which students may use the library and when; in a market, traders allot stall places and so decide who gets the best places; in government, a legislature passes a budget and so decides how public money is shared among services

slides.narration: In a school, a council can fix library hours and decide which students may use the library. In a market, traders allot the best places in the lane. In government, a legislature passes a budget and shares public money among services. In each case, a group decides who gets what.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: sort the situations
slides.body_md: Decide which imagined situations are politics in the wider sense.

rows: A hostel committee decides visiting hours for all residents
A collective decision for a group
A student picks a book to read in her free time
A private choice, not a group decision
Neighbours of Larkspur Lane agree who will pay for a lamp
A club president overrules members and sets all rules alone
Raises how power is used in a group

visual.alt: Worked example table sorting four imagined situations: a hostel committee deciding visiting hours is politics in the wider sense as a collective decision; a student picking a book is not, as a private choice; neighbours agreeing who will pay for a lamp is, as shares are settled together; a club president setting all rules alone is, as it raises the question of how power is used
visual.caption: The hostel, lane and club are imagined.

slides.narration: A hostel committee deciding visiting hours is politics, since a group decides for all residents. A student choosing a book is a private choice. Neighbours agreeing who pays for a lamp settle shares together. A club president who sets all the rules raises the question of how power is used.

slides.heading: Why politics touches everyone

nodes.label: Groups make decisions on shared matters

visual.alt: Flow showing why politics touches everyone: every person belongs to groups, groups make decisions on shared matters, those decisions affect each member, so politics touches everyone
visual.caption: From group life to politics

slides.narration: Every person belongs to groups, such as a family, a school and a community. These groups make decisions on shared matters, and those decisions affect each member. So politics touches everyone, whether or not they join a party or hold an office.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Collective decisions, differences resolved, common goals
The process by which groups decide how to live together, who gets what and how power is used

slides.narration: To sum up. The popular view sees politics as scheming. Aristotle held that humans are political by nature. The wider view sees collective decisions, resolved differences and common goals. Politics is found in the family, the school, the market and the government. It is the process by which groups decide how to live together, who gets what and how power is used.

decks.title: Political Theory: An Introduction, Part 2: What Political Theory Does and Why We Study It
goals: Explain what political theory studies and name its main concepts
Explain how political theory clarifies concepts and tests opinions with reasons
Name the thinkers of political theory with a period and one idea each
Explain how ideals are debated and applied, and why political theory is worth studying

slides.heading: What Political Theory Does
slides.body_md: Part 2: the **ideas** it studies, the **questions** it asks, its **thinkers** and its **uses**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: concepts, questions, thinkers, practice and why we study political theory
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we ask what political theory does. We look at the ideas it studies, the kinds of questions it asks, some of its thinkers, how ideals are debated in practice, and why it is worth studying.

slides.heading: What political theory studies

rows: The ideas and principles that shape constitutions, governments and social life
Freedom, equality, justice, rights, democracy, citizenship, nationalism and secularism
Normative questions about what ought to be, as well as descriptive questions about what is
What does it do with them?
It clarifies concepts, examines their meanings and tests opinions with reasons

visual.alt: Table on what political theory does: it studies the ideas and principles that shape constitutions, governments and social life; it examines concepts such as freedom, equality, justice, rights, democracy, citizenship, nationalism and secularism; it asks normative as well as descriptive questions; and it clarifies concepts, examines meanings and tests opinions with reasons

slides.narration: Political theory studies the ideas and principles that shape constitutions, governments and social life. It examines concepts such as freedom, equality, justice and rights. It asks normative questions about what ought to be, as well as descriptive questions about what is. And it clarifies concepts and tests opinions with reasons.

sections.heading: 1. What is politics?
sections.body_md:
Many people see politics as **manipulation, scheming or the pursuit of self-interest** by politicians. This is the **popular view**. A **wider view** sees politics as the activity through which a society **makes collective decisions, resolves differences and pursues common goals**.

**Aristotle**, a thinker of ancient Greece, held that human beings are **political by nature**: they live in communities and share in decisions about common life.

**Standard definition:** politics is the process by which groups make collective decisions about how to live together, who gets what, and how power is used.

A decision taken by a group that applies to all of its members.
The ability to decide or to influence what a group does.

sections.heading: 2. Politics in every area of life
sections.body_md:
Politics is an aspect of social life that touches everyone. It appears in the **family** (sharing chores and savings), the **school** (council rules, library hours), the **market** (allotting stalls, settling disputes) and the **government** (laws, budgets). A private choice made by one person alone is not a group decision.

Politicians sometimes misuse power, and that deserves criticism. But the need for shared decisions in groups remains, so it is not reasonable to call all politics dirty.

The view that politics is the activity of making collective decisions and settling differences in any group.

sections.heading: 3. What political theory does
sections.body_md:
**Political theory** studies the ideas and principles that shape constitutions, governments and social life: **freedom, equality, justice, rights, democracy, citizenship, nationalism and secularism**.

It asks **normative** questions about what ought to be, as well as **descriptive** questions about what is. It **clarifies concepts**, examines their meanings and **tests our opinions with reasons**. The words ought and should often signal a normative question.

key_terms.definition_md: The study of the ideas and principles that shape constitutions, governments and social life.
A general idea, such as freedom or justice, that we use to think about political life.
A question about what ought to be, which is settled by reasons and principles.
A question about what is the case, which is settled by facts and evidence.

sections.heading: 4. Thinkers of political theory
sections.body_md: Names and one idea each: **Plato** (ancient Greece), justice and the well-ordered state; **Aristotle** (ancient Greece), humans are political beings; **Machiavelli** (16th century), how rulers gain and keep power in practice; **Hobbes** (17th century), a common authority is needed for security; **Locke** (17th century), government rests on consent and protects natural rights; **Rousseau** (18th century), how can life under common rules be consistent with the natural freedom of people; **Marx** (19th century), class conflict and economic arrangements; **Gandhi** (20th century), **Hind Swaraj (1909)**, on self-rule; **Ambedkar** (20th century), social justice and the removal of caste hierarchy.

key_terms.definition_md: A work of Gandhi, written in 1909, that discusses self-rule.
Rights that, in the view of thinkers such as Locke, people hold as human beings, before any government.

sections.heading: 5. Political theory in practice
sections.body_md:
Ideals are **understood in more than one way**, so people differ on how to apply them. Examples of debated questions are the use of **reserved seats**, how to apply **equality between women and men** and the **limits of freedom of expression**. A fair account says that **people differ** and weighs the reasons given.

The **Fundamental Rights** turn ideas into rights: **Article 14** (equality before the law), **Article 17** (abolition of untouchability), **Article 19** (freedom of speech and expression, among other freedoms) and **Article 25** (freedom of conscience and religion).

sections.heading: 6. Why study political theory?
sections.body_md: Everyone is a **citizen** and is affected by politics. The study helps us to **reason about issues** instead of reacting on impulse, to **examine our own prejudices**, and to take part in **democratic debate with tolerance** of other views. It also prepares us for roles in **law, administration and journalism**.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling all politics dirty: separate misuse of power from the need for shared decisions.
- Limiting politics to parties and elections: show that any group which decides together is engaged in politics.
- Mixing up normative and descriptive: look for ought or should, and ask whether the statement can be checked as a fact.
- Naming a thinker without a period or an idea: pair each name with a century and one idea.
- Taking sides on a debated question: write people differ, give the reasons on each side and weigh them.

**Exam tips**
- Give the standard definition of politics in full, with an example from daily life.
- Define normative and descriptive with one example each.
- Cite an Article by number with what it provides.

questions.stem_md: Which statement gives the standard definition of politics as used in political theory?

options.text_md: The work of political parties during election campaigns
The process by which groups make collective decisions about how to live together, who gets what, and how power is used
The effort of an individual to gain personal advantage over others
The study of laws passed by the legislature

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The process by which groups make collective decisions about how to live together, who gets what, and how power is used. Politics covers the whole process of reaching collective decisions in a group, including the sharing of benefits and the use of power. Election campaigns, personal advantage and the study of laws are narrower matters or different things.

questions.stem_md: At Kestrel Hill School, Imran says that politics means scheming by people who want power for themselves. Meera replies that the staff and students who met to decide whether the library should stay open after class were also doing politics. Meera is using

options.text_md: the popular view, in which politics is manipulation by politicians
the legal view, in which politics is the writing of statutes
the economic view, in which politics is the pricing of goods
the wider view, in which politics is any activity of making collective decisions and settling differences

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the wider view, in which politics is any activity of making collective decisions and settling differences. Meera points to a shared decision made by a group that had to settle different wishes, which is the wider view. Imran is the one who holds the popular view of scheming, and neither the legal nor the economic description fits a meeting about the library.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is closest to the idea of Aristotle about human beings and politics?

options.text_md: Humans are by nature beings who live in communities and take part in shared public life
Humans become political only after they enter a political party
Humans are political only when they hold an office
Humans live best when they stay away from all community life

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Humans are by nature beings who live in communities and take part in shared public life. Aristotle held that living with others in a community, and sharing in decisions about common life, belongs to human nature. Joining a party, holding office or withdrawing from community life are not what he meant.

questions.stem_md: Every Sunday the Rao family of Fernwick sits together to decide who will cook, who will clean and how the month's savings will be used, and the members settle their differences by talking and voting. This is an example of politics in the wider sense because

options.text_md: a government official is present at the meeting
the family belongs to a political party
the members make collective decisions, resolve differences and share duties and resources
the meeting is held in a public hall

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the members make collective decisions, resolve differences and share duties and resources. The three features of politics are all present: a group decides together, differences are settled and duties and resources are shared. The presence of an official, a party membership or a public hall is not needed for a group decision to be political in this sense.

questions.stem_md: The stall-holders of the Dunmore weekly market meet to decide how the best spots will be allotted, how disputes over prices will be settled and what fee each stall will pay. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Politics is absent, since no minister is involved
Politics is absent, since markets deal only with money
Politics is present in the market, since a group is deciding who gets what and how disputes are settled
Politics is present only if the town council takes over the meeting

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Politics is present in the market, since a group is deciding who gets what and how disputes are settled. The stall-holders are taking collective decisions about shares and disputes, so the activity is political in the wider sense. The absence of a minister, the fact that money is involved or the later arrival of a council does not alter that.

questions.stem_md: The student council of Pinecrest School must decide whether the canteen will stop selling fried snacks. Some members want the change for health reasons, and others want the snacks kept because they are cheap. The council votes and the rule is adopted. Which element of the definition of politics does the vote mainly illustrate?

options.text_md: A collective decision that settles a difference of views
A court judgment on a legal dispute
The writing of a constitution
The collection of taxes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A collective decision that settles a difference of views. Members who disagreed reached a decision for the whole school by a vote, which is a collective decision settling a difference. A court judgment, a constitution and taxes are not involved.

questions.stem_md: In the debating club of Orchard Vale, the president alone decides which members may speak, which topics are discussed and who may use the club room, and members who object are told to leave. Which part of the definition of politics is most clearly raised by this situation?

options.text_md: How the club will earn money
How the club will choose its colours
How the room will be cleaned
How power is used in a group, and whether it is shared or concentrated

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** How power is used in a group, and whether it is shared or concentrated. The decisions are made by one person, so the question is how power is used and who holds it. Money, colours and cleaning are not the issue in this case, although they may also be decided by the group.

questions.stem_md: A student claims that politics exists only in the offices of the government. Which reply is the most accurate?

options.text_md: The claim is right, since only a government can take collective decisions
Politics also appears wherever groups, such as families, schools and markets, take collective decisions
Politics exists only where elections are held
Politics exists only in the capital city

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Politics also appears wherever groups, such as families, schools and markets, take collective decisions. Collective decisions are made in many kinds of groups, so politics is not confined to government offices, elections or a capital. Governments are one important place for politics but not the only one.

questions.stem_md: The residents of Larkspur Lane meet to agree on a common aim, a safe play area for children, and to decide who will contribute what. Which part of the standard view of politics does the meeting best show?

options.text_md: Pursuing common goals through a collective decision
Conducting a census
Enforcing a court order
Drafting an international treaty

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Pursuing common goals through a collective decision. The residents are working out a shared aim and the contributions each will make, which is pursuing common goals by collective decision. A census, a court order and a treaty are different activities.

questions.stem_md: A newspaper column in imagined Aldmere says that politics is dirty because a few councillors were found to have helped their friends to win contracts. A political theorist would most reasonably respond that

options.text_md: the column proves that all politics is corrupt
misconduct by some office-holders is a fault in how power is used, but it does not make the whole activity of collective decision-making dirty
the councillors were not doing politics
misconduct should not be questioned in a discussion of politics

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** misconduct by some office-holders is a fault in how power is used, but it does not make the whole activity of collective decision-making dirty. Misuse of power by some individuals calls for criticism, yet collective decision-making as such remains necessary in any group. To say that all politics is corrupt generalises from a few cases, and to deny that the councillors were engaged in politics or to forbid questions would not be reasonable.

questions.stem_md: What does political theory study?

options.text_md: Only the dates of important events
Only the results of elections
The ideas and principles, such as freedom, equality and justice, that shape constitutions, governments and social life
Only the budget of a government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The ideas and principles, such as freedom, equality and justice, that shape constitutions, governments and social life. Political theory studies the ideas and principles behind political life and asks what they mean and how they should guide it. Dates, election results and budgets are matters of other kinds of study.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined town of Brookfield, a speaker says, "Every child ought to receive a free midday meal at school." This statement is

options.text_md: descriptive, since it reports what is already done
neither, since it has no reference to society
a statement of a scientific law
normative, since it says what should be done

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** normative, since it says what should be done. The word ought shows that the speaker is saying what should be, so the statement is normative. A descriptive statement would report a fact, and the statement is certainly about society and is not a scientific law.

questions.stem_md: A survey of the imagined district of Marlow reports that 62 out of every 100 eligible voters cast their votes in the last local election. This statement is

options.text_md: normative, since it says what ought to be done
a statement of a value judgment
a prediction about the next election
descriptive, since it reports what is the case

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** descriptive, since it reports what is the case. The survey states a fact about voting that can be checked, which is descriptive. It does not say what ought to be, it passes no judgment of value and it says nothing about the future.

questions.stem_md: Two teams in the Orchard Vale debate club argue about whether a school rule is "fair", but one team means equal treatment of all and the other means treatment suited to each need. According to political theory, the best first step is to

options.text_md: end the debate at once
ask the louder team to speak again
clarify what each team means by fair before judging the rule
count the number of supporters on each side

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** clarify what each team means by fair before judging the rule. Theory begins by examining the meaning of the concept, since the two teams are using one word in two senses. Ending the debate, rewarding loudness or counting supporters would not settle what the word means.

questions.stem_md: A student of Westmere School says, "Our class monitor should be chosen by lots." Which response is an example of testing the opinion with reasons?

options.text_md: "That is a silly idea."
"Lots give each student an equal chance, but they ignore who is able to do the work, so we should weigh these two points."
"Everyone in my row agrees with me."
"I will not discuss the matter."

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** "Lots give each student an equal chance, but they ignore who is able to do the work, so we should weigh these two points.". The first reply states reasons on both sides and weighs them, which is how political theory tests an opinion. Calling an idea silly, pointing to the agreement of a few friends or refusing to discuss offers no reasons.

questions.stem_md: Which of these questions about the imagined republic of Zandria is normative?

options.text_md: Should the vote be given to citizens at an earlier age than it is now?
How many citizens voted in the last election?
In which year was the Zandrian assembly first elected?
How many seats does the Zandrian assembly have?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Should the vote be given to citizens at an earlier age than it is now? Only the first question asks what should be done. The other three ask for facts that can be looked up and so are descriptive.

questions.stem_md: Which thinker of ancient Greece held that human beings are political by nature?

options.text_md: Hobbes
Aristotle
Marx
Locke

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Aristotle. Aristotle of ancient Greece held that human beings are political by nature. Hobbes and Locke belong to the 17th century and Marx to the 19th century.

questions.stem_md: On the imagined island of Tarn-Vey there is no common authority, and the settlers live in fear of one another. They agree to obey one ruler so that they may live in safety. Whose idea about the reasons for government does this story resemble most?

options.text_md: Marx
Ambedkar
Plato
Hobbes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Hobbes. Hobbes reasoned that without a common authority life would be insecure, and that people accept a ruler for the sake of safety. Marx stressed class conflict, Ambedkar the removal of social hierarchy, and Plato the nature of justice and the well-ordered state.

questions.stem_md: The imagined assembly of Mirevale declares that its government rests on the consent of the people and exists to protect their life, liberty and property. Which thinker's idea is closest to this view?

options.text_md: Locke
Machiavelli
Marx
Gandhi

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Locke. Locke argued that people hold natural rights and that government draws its authority from their consent and must protect those rights. Machiavelli studied how rulers keep power, Marx studied class conflict and Gandhi stressed self-rule and non-violence.

questions.stem_md: A writer in the imagined city of Vorenza explains how rulers have actually won and kept power, and sets aside the question of how they ought to behave in an ideal world. Which thinker's approach does this resemble?

options.text_md: Rousseau, who asked about the loss of freedom in society
Gandhi, who wrote Hind Swaraj
Machiavelli, who studied the practice of power
Ambedkar, who worked for social justice

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Machiavelli, who studied the practice of power. Machiavelli of the 16th century is known for looking at how power is gained and held in practice. Rousseau, Gandhi and Ambedkar are linked with other concerns: freedom in society, self-rule, and the removal of social hierarchy.

questions.stem_md: Which question about freedom is associated with Rousseau?

options.text_md: How can the largest army be raised at the lowest cost?
Why should property be distributed equally by the market?
People are free by nature, yet find themselves bound in society, so how can life under common rules be made consistent with freedom?
How can the vote be limited to a small group?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** People are free by nature, yet find themselves bound in society, so how can life under common rules be made consistent with freedom? Rousseau, writing in the 18th century, pointed to a tension between natural freedom and the bonds of society and asked how a society could be arranged so that obedience to rules would not destroy freedom. The other options are not questions that he is known for.

questions.stem_md: Which idea is associated with Marx?

options.text_md: Social change is shaped by economic arrangements and by conflict between classes
The best ruler is always a philosopher
Government rests on a contract that guarantees property
Self-rule begins with the mastery of oneself

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Social change is shaped by economic arrangements and by conflict between classes. Marx, of the 19th century, stressed the part of economic arrangements and class conflict in shaping history. The rule of philosophers is a theme of Plato, the contract on property relates to Locke, and self-rule through self-mastery belongs to Gandhi.

questions.stem_md: Hind Swaraj, a work that discusses self-rule, was written by Gandhi in
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 1909. Gandhi wrote Hind Swaraj in 1909. The other years mark other events and do not belong to the book.

questions.stem_md: Which Article of the Constitution protects, among other freedoms, the freedom of speech and expression?

options.text_md: Article 17
Article 19
Article 14
Article 25

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Article 19. Article 19 gives the freedom of speech and expression, among other freedoms. Article 17 abolishes untouchability, Article 14 provides equality before the law and Article 25 concerns freedom of religion.

questions.stem_md: Which Article abolishes untouchability?

options.text_md: Article 17
Article 19
Article 21
Article 25

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Article 17. Article 17 abolishes untouchability. Article 19 deals with freedoms, Article 21 with life and personal liberty and Article 25 with freedom of religion.

questions.stem_md: Article 14 provides that the state shall not deny any person equality before the law. Which concept of political theory does this provision reflect?

options.text_md: Nationalism
Equality
Secularism only
Federalism

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Equality. A promise of equal treatment before the law applies the concept of equality. Nationalism, secularism and federalism are different concepts, and the provision is not mainly about any of them.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined Pinecrest School, students differ on whether a school bus should give a seat first to the youngest or to those who live farthest away; each side says that its plan is the fairer one. This difference most clearly shows that

options.text_md: fairness has no meaning
only one side can speak in a debate
an ideal such as fairness can be understood and applied in more than one way, which is why it needs reasoned debate
rules for a school bus have nothing to do with ideals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** an ideal such as fairness can be understood and applied in more than one way, which is why it needs reasoned debate. Each side appeals to fairness but applies it differently, which is why ideals call for reasoned discussion. Fairness does have meaning, both sides may argue, and rules about seats do involve ideals.

questions.stem_md: Which is the most suitable way for a student to write about a debated question such as the reservation of seats?

options.text_md: Only one side is honest and the other is not
The question should never be discussed
The most popular opinion must be correct
People differ on this question; some give one set of reasons and others give another, and each can be weighed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** People differ on this question; some give one set of reasons and others give another, and each can be weighed. A fair account gives the reasons put forward by each side and lets the reader weigh them. Declaring one side dishonest, refusing to discuss or treating popularity as proof would not be a reasoned approach.

questions.stem_md: An imagined debating society in Fernwick argues about how equality between women and men should be applied in the sharing of household work. Which feature of political theory does this debate show?

options.text_md: It collects only statistics
It avoids the topic of values
It records only the history of past events
It takes an ideal such as equality and asks how it is to be understood and applied in practice

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It takes an ideal such as equality and asks how it is to be understood and applied in practice. The society is trying to understand and apply an ideal to a real situation, which is the work of political theory. Collecting only statistics, avoiding values or recording past events would not do that.

questions.stem_md: In what way do the Fundamental Rights show the link between political theory and the Constitution?

options.text_md: They are unrelated to any idea of freedom or equality
They list the dates of earlier amendments
They turn ideas such as freedom, equality and justice into rights that people can claim
They describe the powers of the Election Commission

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** They turn ideas such as freedom, equality and justice into rights that people can claim. The Fundamental Rights give concrete form to ideals, so that persons can claim them. They are plainly related to freedom and equality, and they are neither a list of amendment dates nor a description of the Election Commission.

questions.stem_md: A rumour spreads at Westmere School that the principal will cancel the annual sports day. One student calls for a protest at once. Another asks who said it, what the rule actually says and what the effects of each choice would be. The second student shows how political theory helps us to

options.text_md: ignore all rules
reason about an issue with evidence and principles before reacting on impulse
follow the crowd
avoid any decision

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** reason about an issue with evidence and principles before reacting on impulse. Asking for the source, the rule and the likely effects is reasoning about an issue before acting, which is what the study encourages. Ignoring rules, following the crowd and avoiding decisions are not reasoned responses.

questions.stem_md: Tarun finds that he has always assumed that no student from a small village could lead a debate, until he listens to the winning speaker from Kelmarsh. Which benefit of studying political theory does his change of mind illustrate?

options.text_md: It helps us to examine our own prejudices in the light of reasons and experience
It teaches us to defend every old assumption
It makes us avoid people who differ from us
It gives a fixed answer to every question

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It helps us to examine our own prejudices in the light of reasons and experience. Tarun tests an assumption against evidence and gives it up, which is the examination of prejudice. Defending old assumptions, avoiding others or having ready answers would not follow from this study.

questions.stem_md: In the Orchard Vale club, a member who disagrees with the proposal is invited to speak first, and others listen before answering. This practice supports which aim of studying political theory?

options.text_md: Silencing opponents
Democratic debate and tolerance of other views
Choosing a leader by force
Avoiding all discussion

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Democratic debate and tolerance of other views. Giving the dissenting member a hearing is a way of practising democratic debate and tolerance. Silencing, force and avoiding discussion would defeat that aim.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Politics is not limited to the work of governments.

**Reason (R):** Families, schools and markets also make collective decisions that settle differences and share resources.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

2. Aristotle held that human beings are **political by nature** and live in communities.
3. In the wider view, politics is the activity by which a society **makes collective decisions, resolves differences and pursues common goals**.
4. It is found in the **family, school, market and government**.
5. In short, politics is the process by which groups decide how to live together, who gets what and how power is used.

marking_scheme.step: Wider view: collective decisions and goals

questions.stem_md: What does political theory do? Explain with examples.
questions.solution_md: Studies, asks and clarifies.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Political theory is the study of the **ideas and principles** behind constitutions, governments and everyday social arrangements.
2. Among the concepts it examines are **freedom, equality, justice, rights, democracy, citizenship, nationalism and secularism**.
3. Besides descriptive questions about what is, it raises **normative questions** on what ought to be done.
4. It **clarifies the meaning** of concepts, for example what we mean by fair.
5. It **tests opinions with reasons** so that debate rests on arguments.

marking_scheme.step: Normative as well as descriptive questions

questions.stem_md: Describe the ideas of any five thinkers of political theory, with the century of each.
questions.solution_md: Five thinkers with centuries.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Aristotle** (ancient Greece) held that human beings are political by nature and live in communities.
2. **Machiavelli** (16th century) studied how rulers gain and hold power in practice.
3. **Hobbes** (17th century) argued that a common authority is needed so that people can live in security.
4. **Locke** (17th century) argued that government rests on consent and must protect natural rights.
5. **Rousseau** (18th century) asked how freedom can be kept while living under common rules in society.

marking_scheme.step: First thinker with idea and period

questions.stem_md: How are ideals such as freedom and equality debated and applied in practice? Refer to the Fundamental Rights.
questions.solution_md: Debate and constitutional application.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. An ideal can be **read in more than one way**, and so people may differ about how it is to be put into practice.
2. Debates on **reservation, gender equality and freedom of expression** show that people differ on these questions.
3. Each side gives reasons, and political theory asks that they be **weighed**.
4. The **Fundamental Rights** turn ideas into rights, for example **Article 19** on freedom of speech and expression.
5. **Article 14** on equality before the law and **Article 17** abolishing untouchability apply equality and justice.

marking_scheme.step: Ideals can be read in more than one way

questions.stem_md: Why should we study political theory? Give five reasons.
questions.solution_md: Five reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Every person is a **citizen** who lives under collective decisions and is affected by politics.
2. The study helps us to **reason about issues** with evidence and principles instead of reacting on impulse.
3. It helps us to **examine our own prejudices** and to revise them when reasons require.
4. It prepares us for roles and careers in **law, administration and journalism**.
5. It supports **democratic debate and tolerance** of views that differ from our own.

questions.stem_md: Explain the difference between descriptive and normative questions with imagined examples from a school council, and say why political theory needs both.
questions.solution_md: Two kinds of question, and why both matter.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A **descriptive** question asks what is the case, for example how many students use the canteen.
2. A **normative** question asks what ought to be, for example whether the canteen ought to stop selling fried snacks.
3. Descriptive answers rest on **facts** that can be checked.
4. Normative answers rest on **values and reasons** that must be argued.
5. Political theory needs both, since **facts inform** a decision while **values guide** what to do.

Dear Hamid,
You say that politics is nothing but cheating and that studying it is a waste of time. I used to think so too. But in our class we had to decide how to share the use of the school's single computer room, and it showed me how a group makes a decision. We also had to ask what we meant by a fair share. When I looked at my first opinion again, I found that I had judged all politicians by a few I had read about.
Yours, Sana

children.stem_md: Which view of politics does Hamid hold?

answer.model_answer_md: The **popular view**, that politics is cheating and manipulation.

children.stem_md: Which activity in the letter shows political theory clarifying a concept?

answer.model_answer_md: Asking **what is meant by a fair share** of the computer room.

marking_scheme.step: Asking what a fair share means

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Which benefit of studying political theory does Sana's last sentence show? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: It shows that the study helps us to **examine our own prejudices**. Sana saw that she had **judged all politicians** by a few examples and revised her opinion with reasons.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Write two points that Sana might add to persuade Hamid that the study is useful.

answer.model_answer_md: It helps us **reason about issues** before reacting, and it prepares us for roles such as **law, administration and journalism**. It also supports **respectful debate** among people who differ.
